paper_metadata.title: Application of an upsampling algorithm to quantum state preparation of continuous and discrete probability distributions

summary: The paper proposes an upsampling-based gate-model quantum algorithm for preparing quantum states whose amplitudes correspond to sampled probability distributions. Example simulations prepare Gaussian and Laplace distributions with n = 3 qubits and a binomial distribution with n = 4 qubits; the original divide‑and‑conquer circuit has exponential depth but can be transformed via quantum forking to polylogarithmic depth at the cost of 2^n − 1 ancilla qubits.

experiments.description: Gate-based quantum state preparation via an upsampling/divide-and-conquer circuit for continuous probability distributions, demonstrated on Gaussian and Laplace distributions and converted to a polylogarithmic-depth quantum-forking circuit.

algorithm.variant: upsampling quantum state preparation; divide-and-conquer circuit transformed to quantum forking

hyperparameters.qubit_count_n: varies; examples use n=3 for Gaussian and Laplace simulations

algorithm.parameter_initialization: not specified; state-preparation angles computed analytically from the target distribution

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Prepare an n-qubit state whose amplitudes are square roots of sampled probabilities from a continuous PDF over R; computational basis states map to sampled points x_n via x_n = x_0 + Delta x_n * i_n
problem_formulation.objective_function: Prepare |psi_n> = sum_i sqrt(P(x_i) delta_x) |i> with amplitudes proportional to sampled PDF values
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Normalization via delta_xn; periodic extension of the PDF over the sampling window; no optimization constraints

problem_instance.description: Univariate continuous probability distributions on the real line; examples shown for Gaussian and Laplace distributions, with lognormal mentioned as a mapped example
problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Discretize the continuous PDF on a sampling window of width w; choose sampling interval Delta x_n = w/2^n; optionally shift window by zeta to avoid aliasing
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: State-vector preparation illustrated by sampling/measurement plots and circuit diagrams; no statistical benchmarking protocol reported

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Analytical computation of rotation angles from the target PDF; sampling-window discretization
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Measurement probabilities compared to target distribution plots

results.unit: qualitative: exponential for direct divide-and-conquer circuit; polylogarithmic after quantum forking

speedup_claims.factor: polylogarithmic gate depth after quantum forking; exponential depth for the direct divide-and-conquer circuit
speedup_claims.conditions: using quantum forking transformation; no numeric benchmark reported
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper reports qualitative complexity only and does not provide measured runtime, gate counts, or a classical runtime baseline.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: polylogarithmic gate depth after quantum forking; exponential depth for the direct divide-and-conquer circuit

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Would require large-scale fault-tolerant quantum hardware implementing the quantum-forking circuit with O(polylog N) depth and substantial ancilla overhead (≈2^n ancilla qubits for n data qubits).
limiting_factors: No comparison with classical algorithms for probability distribution sampling or state preparation
Quantum forking requires exponential ancilla overhead (2^n − 1 ancilla qubits)
No quantitative runtime or gate-count evaluation

notes: Hardware inferred as simulator_statevector because the paper presents simulations and circuit diagrams but names no physical QPU/device.
n=3 is explicitly stated for the Gaussian and Laplace example circuits in the figure captions.
Depth is reported qualitatively: exponential for the original circuit and polylogarithmic after quantum forking; no numeric depth is given.
The authors do not claim quantum advantage over classical algorithms; they present a quantum circuit construction and a depth-reduction technique.
All results are circuit simulations illustrating probability distributions.

experiments.description: Gate-based quantum state preparation for a discrete probability distribution, demonstrated on a binomial distribution using the same upsampling framework and its quantum-forking conversion.

algorithm.variant: upsampling quantum state preparation for discrete probabilities; binomial example

hyperparameters.qubit_count_n: n=4 in the figure caption for the binomial example

algorithm.parameter_initialization: not specified; angles derived analytically from discrete probabilities

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Prepare a state whose amplitudes are square roots of discrete probabilities P(k,l); the paper notes a special construction using an auxiliary complementary-probability state for n>1
problem_formulation.objective_function: Prepare |psi_n> with amplitudes sqrt(P(in)) for a discrete distribution
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Normalization by construction; auxiliary complementary state used to fit the divide-and-conquer circuit form

problem_instance.description: Discrete binomial distribution over k in {0,...,l}
problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: No data preprocessing beyond mapping discrete probabilities into the state-preparation circuit
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Projection of the most significant qubit shown in the figure caption; no formal benchmarking protocol reported

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Analytical derivation of discrete-probability rotation angles from the binomial distribution
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Measurement/projection of the most significant qubit to visualize the binomial distribution

results.unit: qualitative: exponential for direct divide-and-conquer circuit; polylogarithmic after quantum forking

speedup_claims.factor: polylogarithmic gate depth after quantum forking; exponential depth for the direct divide-and-conquer circuit
speedup_claims.conditions: using quantum forking transformation; no numeric benchmark reported
speedup_claims.caveats: No empirical speedup or classical baseline is reported; only asymptotic circuit-depth improvement is claimed.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: polylogarithmic gate depth after quantum forking; exponential depth for the direct divide-and-conquer circuit

limiting_factors: Demonstration limited to a small simulated binomial distribution (n = 4)
Ancilla overhead scales as 2^n − 1 in the quantum forking construction
No empirical runtime or hardware evaluation
